=== FINDINGS FROM deepseek_deepseek-v4-pro ===
- tests/test_review_conflict_resolve_retry_prelude_render.py:530-605 | severity=BLOCKER | confidence=5
  PROBLEM: test_out_of_scope_attempt_restores_before_retry (line 530) and test_unsafe_attempt_restore_stops_beforesecond_attempt (line 560) exercise the capture/check/restore Python heredoc behavior in a real git sandbox. Neither function is called from main() (lines 584-605). Only test_scope_check_precedes_retry_success_and_preserves_final_guard (line 575) is wired, and that test only asserts string ordering in the shell script — it never executes the Python logic. The test file runs via direct python3 execution (ci.yml:735, mark-stable.yml:360, test-and-mark-stble.yml:4169), and main() is the sole entry point (lines 608-609). Both behavioral tests are dead code.
  WHY: CI passes green even if the Python heredoc capture/check/restore logic is completely broken. No test executes the actual behavior.
- scripts/review_conflict_resolve.sh:1945-1949 | severity=NIT | confidence=3
  PROBLEM: On retries, _restore_attempt_base failure is now fatal (exit 1) instead of the previous "echo ::warning:: ...; continuing". For the source-repo full-tree path this is the intended behavior (lines 904-906 delegate to _resolver_attempt_state restore which returns non-zero on unsafe state). For consumer repos the same fatal path now applies — the old per-file allowlist restore (lines 908-919) can return non-zero if any cp -a fails, which was previously non-fatal but now stops the retry loop entirely.
  WHY: A consumer-repo with a corrupted allowlist snapshot where cp -a fails on one file now exits the entire retry loop instead of loging a warning and retrying with the best-effort state. This is the safer direction (refusing to commit when state is untrusted) but differs from the old behavior.
- Requirement: "Extend an existing resolver retry test to cover both a recovered scope violation and an unsafe restore." (linked issue Suggested fix)
  Expected change site: tests/test_review_conflict_resolve_retry_prelude_render.py main() function, lines 584-605
  Evidence of absence: test_out_of_scope_attempt_restores_before_retry (line 530) and test_unsafe_attempt_restore_stops_beforesecond_attempt (line 560) are defined but are not added to main(). Only test_scope_check_precedes_retry_success_and_preserves_final_guard is wired at line 598.
  SEVERITY: BLOCKER
  ISSUE_CONFIDENCE: 5
- Requirement: "In scripts/review_conflict_resolve.sh, check each attempt's touched paths against the captured CONFLICTED_PATHS_FILE before accepting soft-validation success. On a violation, report the paths, restore and verify the complete pre-attempt state—including out-of-scope edits—and retry within the existing attempt limit; fail closed if restoration is unsafe." (linked issue Suggested fix, second paragraph)
  Expected change site: scripts/review_conflict_resolve.sh — the scope check (line 2138), full-tree capture (line 730), and full-tree restore in _restore_attempt_base (line 904)
  Evidence of absence: All three sites are gated on `if [ "${IS_WORKFLOW_SOURCE_REPO:-false}" = "true" ]`. Consumer repos (IS_WORKFLOW_SOURCE_REPO=false, set by scripts/stage_workflow_support.sh) get none of the pre-acceptance scope check, full-tree restore, or retry-on-violation behavior. They retain the original bug: an out-of-scope edit is accepted by soft validation and fails only at the final check_resolver_diff.sh gate (line ~2632, ungated) after the retry loop has ended. The issue's suggested fix names no source-repo-only restriction. The final hard gate is preserved for all repos, so a consumer-repo resolver still rejects the bad commit rather than pushing it — it just cannot retry via the new scope-violation path.
  SEVERITY: MAJOR
  ISSUE_CONFIDENCE: 4

  Issue: shutil is imported but never referenced in the heredoc.

- scripts/review_conflict_resolve.sh:_resolver_attempt_state(), lines 597-625; _restore_attempt_base, line 904; _resolver_attempt_state check, line 2138 | severity=MAJOR | confidence=4

  WHY: A repository with thousands of files will incur a significant performance penalty on every attempt, effectively doubling the I/O cost (capture + restore) and potentially timing out large resolution tasks on environments with high I/O latency.
